newsitem.title: FRANCE: TENNIS-HOLDER SAMPRAS LEADS PROCESSION OF SKITTLED SEEDS.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-HOLDER SAMPRAS LEADS PROCESSION OF SKITTLED SEEDS.

text.p: Defending champion Pete Sampras was swept out of the Paris Open in straight sets by Switzerland's Marc Rosset on Wednesday, one of nine seeded players to crash out in his opening match.

Top seed Sampras followed the downfall of Boris Becker, Goran Ivanisevic, Thomas Muster, Marcelo Rios and Alberto Costa, continuing the exodus of stars which started the previous day when Richard Krajicek, Jim Courier and Andre Agassi were beaten.
Rosset, a finalist in 1994, took only 75 minutes to upstage Sampras 6-4 6-4, while sixth seed Becker fell in three sets to Spain's Carlos Moya 6-3 5-7 6-4 in what he called a "madhouse" atmosphere.
Ivanisevic, the fifth seed, crashed out 6-3 6-2 to Dutchman Paul Haarhuis and number three Muster succumbed to a nagging hip complaint, retiring after dropping the first set 6-2 to Stefan Edberg.

Dutch qualifier Fernon Wibier extended his remarkable run by eliminating Costa, the 14th seed, 3-6 6-4 6-4, and Czech veteran Petr Korda eliminated 10th-seeded Chilean Marcelo Rios in the last second round match 6-3 6-4 in exactly one hour.
But number four Yevgeny Kafelnikov of Russia, American MaliVai Washington and Thomas Enqvist of Sweden, number 13 and 12 respectively, did make it through to the third round.
French Open champion Kafelnikov needed three sets to get past French hope Cedric Pioline 6-4 3-6 6-4, while Washington beat Czech Martin Damm 6-4 6-2 in 62 minutes.
Enqvist disposed of American Richey Reneberg 6-4 7-5 and now meets Becker's conqueror Moya.
Sampras had never lost to Rosset in four previous meetings, including the third round of the Paris Open in 1993.
The American made no excuses, unlike a disappointed Becker, three times a winner in five finals, who likened the crowd at Bercy to a zoo.
Instead he put it down to the dominant serving of his opponent.

"He's six foot seven (2.01 metres) and it feels like he's slam-dunking on you all the time," Sampras said, employing a basketball term to describe the thundering serves of the lanky Swiss, who sent down 20 aces in the 75-minute match.
Becker, who beat Sampras in Sunday's Stuttgart Open final, was also unable to transfer his form from Germany to France.
"Coming from a very relaxed atmosphere (in Stuttgart) to a madhouse...that caught me completely off guard," he said.
"I felt like I was in a big zoo. Moya and me, we were big gorillas and all around us were some other animals trying to bother us all the time," the world number three said.
"I'm extremely disappointed. I mean, I'm still in a state of shock because even though I've played here a couple of times I didn't think it was like that.
"If people are constantly moving, screaming, laughing, getting up, it's impossible to play great tennis. Tennis is not basketball."
Becker could now fail to qualify to defend his ATP Tour World Championship title in Hanover next month. He needed to reach the semifinals to ensure a berth in the eight-man event.
Edberg, who meets Wibier next, would probaby have preferred a different way of maintaining his 100 percent record against Muster, who he has now beaten 10 times.

But the Swedish veteran, who is quitting at the end of the season, enjoyed the same sort of fortune when he won at Bercy in 1990. On that occasion it was Becker who retired hurt at 3-3 in the opening set.
